newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE, SON OF A LEGEND, CLOSES IN ON GLORY.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE, SON OF A LEGEND, CLOSES IN ON GLORY.

text.p: Jacques Villeneuve will make motor racing history on Sunday if he wins the Japanese Grand Prix to become the first man to lift the IndyCar and Formula One world drivers' titles in successive seasons.
The 25-year-old Canadian will also be one of the youngest champions and the first to claim the drivers' crown in his rookie year.
They are all feats his legendary father Gilles Villeneuve would have been proud to enjoy if he had not been killed when his Ferrari crashed during practice for the 1982 Belgian Grand Prix.

Jacques, introverted and serious, has driven under the shadow of his father's reputation throughout his career, but rarely speaks of him and has made it clear that he is racing for himself and not to prolong a family tradition.

Born in St Jean sur Richelieu, Quebec, on April 9, 1971, Villeneuve grew up in nomadic conditions as his racing and speed-crazed father took part in snowmobile racing in the winter and road racing in the summer all across Canada and the United States.
He took his family with him in caravans and mobile homes, his wife Joann acting as timekeeper and childminder to Jacques and his sister Melanie while he set about establishing his reputation.
Gilles earned fame for his speed and his spectacular style of driving and, after testing with McLaren, joined Ferrari where he won six of his 67 Grands Prix before his death at Zolder.

By then, the family, including Jacques, were living in France and then Monaco. Jacques was sent to boarding school in Switzerland after his father died, but left at 17 to begin his racing career in Italy in Touring Cars.

In 1988 he had three races in an Alfa Romeo without creating much of an impression before embarking on three seasons in Italian Formula Three. It was not until he subsequently raced in Japanese Formula Three series in 1992 that he began to be known for anything other than his sponsor-attractive surname.

He finished second in the Japanese series, winning three races, before moving back to north America and taking part in the Toyota Atlantic Championship in 1993. There he took seven pole positions and won five of the 15 races and was named rookie of the year.

The following season, he stepped up to Indycar racing and became Indycar rookie of the year, scoring his first win at Elkhart Lake and finishing an extraordinary second in the Indianapolis 500 at his first attempt. He finished sixth overall in the championship.
In 1995, he made his big breakthrough to international stardom and acclaim by winning both the Indianapolis 500 and the drivers' championship, claiming four victories and six poles on the way.

By mid-season, it was clear he was a hot property and the Formula One giants Williams gave him a test and signed him. He tested during the 1995-96 off-season in readiness for his first crack at the formula in which his father made his name.
Jacques almost won the opening race, the Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne, where he finished second to Williams team mate Damon Hill.

Since then, the pair have waged a year-long scrap for the title with Villeneuve, known for his scruffy "grunge" appearance and low-key image, building his challenge to a crescendo in the opening races.

Single but close to a long-time girlfriend, fellow-Canadian Sandrine Gros d'Aillon, Villeneuve enjoys skiing, music, reading and computers and has a reputation for impulsive outbursts of wild behaviour when he casts off his serious mask.
In Sunday's race, he will need to win and hope that Hill fails to score a point to take the title.

But judging by the spectacular way in which he passed German double world champion Michael Schumacher's Ferrari on the outside at Estoril during the Portuguese Grand Prix three weeks ago, he has both the courage and the audacity to do it.
